+# ADR-0001: Raise Pricing Cache TTL
+
+## Status
+Accepted
+
+## Context
+
+Our pricing service caches responses at the HTTP level to reduce load on backend systems and improve response latency for clients. The pricing data has been observed to change infrequently in production—updates are typically batch operations coordinated at known intervals, and dynamic repricing events are rare. The current cache TTL of 900 seconds (15 minutes) creates unnecessary cache invalidations and requires clients to re-fetch pricing data roughly every quarter hour, even when the underlying data has not changed.
+
+Analysis of our pricing update patterns shows that most changes cluster around monthly renewal cycles and promotional periods, which occur on predictable schedules. Increasing the cache TTL would significantly reduce redundant requests to the backend while still providing acceptable freshness for business purposes. The tradeoff between cache efficiency and data freshness is well-understood and manageable with our current operational model.
+
+## Decision
+
+We have decided to raise the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This change will be implemented at the HTTP response layer, allowing intermediate caches and client-side caching behaviors to honor the extended TTL. The decision applies to all pricing endpoints unless an endpoint has specific freshness requirements, in which case it will be documented and exempted explicitly.
+
+This decision is reversible and can be tuned further based on operational data. If pricing changes become more frequent or client-facing freshness requirements tighten, the TTL can be adjusted downward without architectural changes.
+
+## Consequences
+
+The extended TTL will reduce backend load by an estimated 75% for pricing-related requests, as most clients will hit cached responses instead of generating backend queries. This improves system reliability during traffic spikes and reduces operational costs. Response times for cached requests improve further, enhancing the user experience.
+
+On the tradeoff side, pricing information visible to clients will be stale by up to one hour after a change. This is acceptable for most use cases, but any real-time pricing features or scenarios requiring immediate consistency across clients should bypass the cache or implement shorter TTLs at the endpoint level. Teams deploying pricing changes must coordinate around the cache window to avoid client confusion, and we should monitor cache hit rates to detect if this TTL proves too aggressive as business practices evolve.
